topics.name: Current, resistance, and resistivity

topics.name: Series, parallel, and Kirchhoff's rules

guide.title: Electric circuits: review guide
guide.intro: Circuits put charge to work. This unit uses conservation of charge and energy, written as Kirchhoff's rules, to find currents and potential differences in networks of resistors and capacitors.
guide.equationNote: Batteries and wires are ideal (no internal resistance) unless a question says otherwise. ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²).

sections.title: Current, resistance, and resistivity
body: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point: I = ΔQ/Δt, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s). Charge is conserved, so in a single loop the current is the same everywhere.
Resistance depends on the material and the shape: R = ρL/A. Ohm's law, ΔV = IR, relates the potential difference across a resistor to the current through it. Power is P = IΔV = I²R = (ΔV)²/R.
points: Longer wires have more resistance and thicker wires have less. A wire's cross-sectional area grows with the square of its diameter.
Resistivity ρ is a property of the material (and its temperature), not of the wire's shape.
A bulb's brightness depends on the power it uses.

sections.title: Series, parallel, and Kirchhoff's rules
body: Junction rule (conservation of charge): the total current into a junction equals the total current out. Loop rule (conservation of energy): the potential differences around any closed loop add to zero.

Resistors in series carry the same current, and their resistances add: R = R₁ + R₂ + …. Resistors in parallel have the same potential difference, and 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …, so the equivalent resistance is smaller than any single branch.
points: Reduce a circuit step by step: combine parallel groups, then series groups, then work back out to each resistor.
With an ideal battery, each parallel branch works independently: removing one branch does not change the others.
Series resistors share the battery's potential difference in proportion to their resistances.

sections.title: Capacitors and RC circuits
body: A capacitor stores separated charge: Q = CΔV. A parallel-plate capacitor has C = κε₀A/d, so larger plates, closer plates, or a dielectric between them increase C. The stored energy is U = ½QΔV = ½C(ΔV)².

In an RC circuit, an uncharged capacitor first acts like a plain wire, so the current starts at ΔV/R. Once fully charged it acts like a break in the circuit, and the current falls to zero. The time constant τ = RC sets how quickly this happens.
points: Capacitors in parallel add: C = C₁ + C₂. In series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
After about 5τ a capacitor is essentially fully charged or fully discharged.
No charge crosses the gap: charge flows onto one plate and off the other.

example.prompt: A 9.0 V battery drives current through a 2.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 4.0 Ω resistors. Find the current from the battery and the current in each 4.0 Ω resistor.
example.solution: The parallel pair is equivalent to 2.0 Ω, so the total resistance is 4.0 Ω and I = 9.0 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 2.25 A. By the junction rule, the current splits equally between the identical branches: about 1.1 A each.

misconceptions: “Current is used up as it flows through resistors.”
Charge is conserved, so the current is the same everywhere in a single loop; energy, not charge, is transferred.
“Adding a resistor in parallel increases the total resistance.”
It adds another path, so the equivalent resistance decreases.
An ideal battery supplies a fixed potential difference; the current depends on the circuit.
Charge builds up on the plates; none crosses between them.

questions.prompt: A current of 2.0 A flows in a wire for 30 s. How much charge passes a point in the wire?
choiceExplanations: 15 C divides the time by the current; charge is current multiplied by time.
0.067 C divides the current by the time.
32 C adds the current and the time, which have different units.

questions.prompt: A wire has resistance R. A second wire of the same material is twice as long and has twice the diameter. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation: R = ρL/A. Doubling the length doubles R. Doubling the diameter multiplies the area by 2² = 4, which divides R by 4. Together: R × 2/4 = R/2.
choiceExplanations: 2R accounts for the longer length but not for the thicker wire.
R treats the area as doubling, but area grows with the square of the diameter, so it quadruples.
R/4 accounts for the larger area but not for the doubled length.

questions.prompt: A bulb uses 60 W when connected to 120 V. What are the current through it and its resistance?
choiceExplanations: 2.0 A is ΔV/P, the ratio upside down; P = IΔV gives I = P/ΔV.
The current is right, but 0.0042 Ω is I/ΔV; resistance is ΔV/I.
7200 A multiplies power by voltage; current is power divided by voltage.

questions.prompt: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series to an 18 V battery. What is the current in the circuit?
questions.explanation: In series the resistances add: 3.0 + 6.0 = 9.0 Ω. I = 18 V ÷ 9.0 Ω = 2.0 A.
choiceExplanations: 9.0 A uses the parallel combination, 2.0 Ω; these resistors are in series.
6.0 A uses only the 3.0 Ω resistor; in series the current passes through both.
0.50 A is R/ΔV, the ratio upside down.

questions.prompt: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel to an 18 V battery. What is the total current from the battery?
questions.explanation: Each branch has the full 18 V across it: 18/3.0 = 6.0 A and 18/6.0 = 3.0 A. By the junction rule the battery supplies 6.0 + 3.0 = 9.0 A (equivalently, 18 V ÷ 2.0 Ω).
choiceExplanations: 2.0 A treats the resistors as if they were in series.
6.0 A is the current in the 3.0 Ω branch only.
3.0 A is the current in the 6.0 Ω branch only.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and official topics come from the linked College Board page, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-10-09); that page was used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: At a junction, 5.0 A flows in through one wire and 2.0 A flows out through a second wire. What is the current in the third wire?
questions.explanation: Junction rule: current in = current out. 5.0 A = 2.0 A + I, so 3.0 A must flow out through the third wire.
choiceExplanations: 3.0 A in would make 8.0 A in and only 2.0 A out, which breaks conservation of charge.
7.0 A out would make 9.0 A out with only 5.0 A in.
7.0 A in adds the two given currents instead of balancing them.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery is connected to a 2.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of resistors, 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. What is the potential difference across the 2.0 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: The parallel pair is equivalent to (6.0 × 3.0)/(6.0 + 3.0) = 2.0 Ω, so the total resistance is 4.0 Ω and I = 12 ÷ 4.0 = 3.0 A. Across the 2.0 Ω resistor, ΔV = IR = 3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0 V; by the loop rule the parallel pair gets the other 6.0 V.
choiceExplanations: 2.2 V treats the 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω resistors as if they were in series (11 Ω in total).
4.0 V splits the 12 V equally among three resistors, but they do not share it equally.
12 V is the whole battery; the loop rule shares it between the resistor and the parallel pair.

questions.prompt: Two identical bulbs are connected in parallel across an ideal battery. One bulb burns out. What happens to the other bulb?
questions.explanation: With an ideal battery, each parallel branch has the full battery voltage across it whatever the other branch does. The working bulb keeps the same voltage, current, and power, so its brightness does not change. (The battery supplies less total current.)
choiceExplanations: The current that went to the burned-out bulb is not redirected; each branch's current is set by its own voltage and resistance.
Its voltage stays equal to the battery voltage, so its power stays the same.
It is on its own complete path to the battery, so it stays lit.

questions.prompt: A 4.0 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. How much charge is on each plate?
choiceExplanations: 3.0 μC is ΔV/C; charge is capacitance multiplied by potential difference.
0.33 μC is C/ΔV.
288 is ½C(ΔV)² = 288 μJ, the stored energy, not the charge.

questions.prompt: The plates of an air-filled parallel-plate capacitor are pulled twice as far apart. What happens to its capacitance?
choices: It becomes one quarter as large
questions.explanation: C = ε₀A/d, so doubling the plate separation d halves the capacitance.
choiceExplanations: A larger gap reduces the capacitance, because d is in the denominator.
Capacitance depends on the plate area and separation, so changing d changes C.
C is proportional to 1/d, not 1/d².

questions.prompt: An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a resistor R, a battery of potential difference ΔV, and an open switch. The switch is closed. How does the current change over time?
choices: It starts at ΔV/R and decreases toward zero
It starts at zero and increases toward ΔV/R
It stays at ΔV/R the whole time
It is zero the whole time, because charge cannot cross the capacitor's gap
questions.explanation: At first the uncharged capacitor has no potential difference across it, so the whole ΔV is across R and I = ΔV/R. As charge builds up on the plates, the capacitor's potential difference grows, the resistor's shrinks, and the current falls toward zero.
choiceExplanations: This is backward: the current is largest at the start, when the capacitor has no charge to oppose the battery.
The current changes because the capacitor's potential difference grows as it charges.
No charge crosses the gap, but charge does flow onto one plate and off the other, so there is a current while the capacitor charges.

questions.prompt: How much energy is stored in a 10 μF capacitor charged to 20 V?
choiceExplanations: 4.0 × 10⁻³ J is C(ΔV)², without the factor ½.
2.0 × 10⁻⁴ is CΔV, which is the charge in coulombs, not the energy.
1.0 × 10⁻⁴ J is ½CΔV; the potential difference must be squared.
